newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian politician quits over corruption scandal.
newsitem.headline: Indian politician quits over corruption scandal.

text.p: A scandal-tainted Indian politician who has transfixed the nation for weeks resigned on Friday as chief minister of the eastern state of Bihar after his arrest was first ordered and then stayed.
In a sign that Laloo Prasad Yadav's exit did not mean the end of the controversy, his supporters promptly rubber-stamped his wife Rabri Devi as his successor.

Prime Minister Inder Kumar Gujral's United Front coalition, which has been badly divided on whether to admit into its fold Yadav's breakaway political faction formed from Gujral's Janata Dal party, decided later on Friday not to admit the group.

"The decision is not to give membership to the Rashtriya Janata Dal (RJD), Information and Broadcasting Minister Jaipal Reddy told reporters after a meeting of senior leaders of the 15-party alliance in the Indian capital.
But a decision on the future of three federal ministers in Yadav's camp, whose political status was undecided for three weeks, had been left to Gujral, he said.

Yadav formed his group earlier this month over internal party differences, but a corruption case involving alleged embezzlement of state animal welfare funds overshadowed his claims to stay on in the coalition.
Yadav, who says he is innocent, resigned after a special court issued arrest warrants against him and three other politicians in the $280-million scandal.
The Supreme Court said he should not be arrested until July 29 when it hears his appeal against the detention order.
Rabri Devi's election invited criticism from opposition leaders who said she was too inexperienced.
"I am happy," Yadav's wife, a 45-year-old mother of nine said nervously. "I will pursue the policies of the Laloo government. Social justice will be the priority."
Bihar is India's second most populous state and one of its poorest regions.

The charismatic Yadav had stubbornly refused to resign since his indictment by the Central Bureau of Investigation in April, resisting legal and political pressures and sparking a national debate on corruption.
"I did not want to create a constitutional crisis and people at the top had become critical of my stand not to resign," Yadav told reporters after his wife took office.
"Now I am free and I am ready to go to jail," he added. "The political and legal battle will go on."
Yadav's intransigence sparked a parliamentary uproar and a national debate on the conduct of leaders, and rattled stock markets.
Friday's drama overshadowed the swearing-in of India's 10th president, K.R. Narayanan, who called for action to root out "the demon of corruption."
"Today there are signs of a weakening of the moral and spiritual fibre in our public life with the evils of communalism, casteism, violence and corruption bedevilling our society," Narayanan said.
Opposition lawmakers pressing for action against Yadav walked out of parliament's upper house while the lower house was angrily debating the scandal.
The Yadav news shook India's premier Bombay Stock Exchange, which fell sharply but then recovered some ground to close 36.76 points, or 0.87 percent, down at 4189.81.
